claims.text: The proposed material is a high-entropy alloy in which Ti and Ni are the dominant constituents.
Conventional melting and casting will ensure that Ti and Ni remain the dominant constituents.
Adding approximately 5 at% Nb and aging at 700 °C for 4–6 hours will form uniformly distributed nanoscale coherent Nb-rich precipitates.
Isothermal aging can mobilize precipitate-forming species and promote precipitation.
Adding Nb increases the local mixing enthalpy of the Ti–Ni-primary alloy.
The Nb-induced change in local mixing enthalpy stimulates nucleation of fine Nb-rich precipitates during aging.
Fine precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
The proposed Nb-rich precipitates retard grain-boundary sliding.
The Nb-added and aged alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the alloy without Nb.
The Nb-added and aged alloy will have greater elevated-temperature creep resistance than the alloy without Nb.
The intervention is applicable at service temperatures up to approximately 800 °C.
Keeping Nb near 5 at% preserves Ti and Ni as the primary constituents.
Excessive aging or unsuitable aging parameters can coarsen the precipitates and reduce their strengthening benefit.
Precipitation strengthening is a robust strengthening mechanism.
The optimum aging time and temperature for balancing precipitate formation and stability are not yet known.
The long-term stability of the proposed precipitate dispersion during prolonged high-temperature exposure is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes comparison with an identically processed alloy without Nb, and the experiment specifies the same processing for the control, but the baseline explicitly omits both Nb and the subsequent aging treatment. Omitting aging from the baseline confounds the effects of Nb addition and aging and is inconsistent with the stated matched control.
